title: NLnet Publishes More Stringent Generative AI Policy
content:
NLnet Publishes More Stringent Generative AI Policy
NLnet has published a new version of its generative AI policy (version 2.0). The revised policy is more restrictive than prior versions, stemming from the foundation's practical experience with thousands of applications processed since the previous policy was published. Generative AI can no longer be used for writing proposals - with the noted exception of supporting accessibility needs. For project development the use of LLMs and diffusion models is confined to read-only usage. These limitations will drastically simplify and speed up evaluation of proposals and work delivered, and allow the foundation to spend more time on actual grantees.
Our new policy is first and foremost a pragmatic measure towards self-protection. Last year we left our processes open to moderate use of LLMs and similar deep-learning systems in case their use was clearly documented, but the result of this experiment has been underwhelming and overwhelming at the same time
, says Michiel Leenaars, director of Strategy at NLnet foundation. We found ourselves having to process an avalanche of additional proposals lacking maturity and relevance. Upon closer inspection, proposals involving AI were on the whole of much lower quality than we are used to at NLnet - and at the same time very taxing and demotivating for our experts to wade through
, says Leenaars.
We recognise there is plenty of potential for generative AI for a variety of use cases
, Leenaars comments. We are not trying to make a more general point about quality, ethical consideration, or security, nor are we making decisions or recommendations for others on whether the use of agents will work for their use cases. It is just that for our particular domain of digital infrastructure and at this point in time, the actual yield turns out to not be worth the additional effort.
How does the new policy affect applicants and grantees?
- The updated policy is effective immediately, and applies to all open calls from NLnet which have their deadline later than the publication date of the new policy. This includes the upcoming calls of Restack and CodeSupply, which have their first deadline on November 3rd 2026.
- Applicants who already put in proposals for these programmes prior to the deadline (against NLnet's recommendation), are urgently advised to check their eligibility with the new policy. If applicants find their proposal or approach is not compatible with the new policy, they may simply update their proposal to comply with the new policy before the deadline. Applicants should follow the regular process for this, meaning they simply resubmit a revised proposal through the application form - preferably mentioning their current proposal ID. Applicants can resubmit any number of times until the deadline has passed.
- (Update for clarification): Applications written with the aid of AI submitted before October 20, 2026, need not be resubmitted. Resubmission is only needed if what is proposed in the application, is not in accordance with the new policy. Having written the application itself with AI prior to the new policy, is not a problem.
- There is a transitional arrangement for applicants and beneficiaries from programmes which are in a concluding phase (notably NGI Zero Commons Fund, NGI Taler and Fediversity). Proposals still under evaluation for those funds will be treated as per the previous (v1.1) version of the GenAI policy out of clemency, but may choose to voluntarily follow the new revised policy in the light of future applications.

report.summary: NLnet tightens its generative AI policy, banning AI-written proposals except for accessibility and limiting project development to read-only LLM and diffusion-model use.
report.background: NLnet Foundation is a Dutch funder of open-source digital infrastructure and a key backer of Next Generation Internet projects, including NGI Zero, NGI Taler and Fediversity. It runs open calls that attract thousands of applications from developers and researchers. Under its previous generative AI policy (v1.1), NLnet allowed moderate, clearly documented use of LLMs and similar deep-learning systems in proposals and projects. After processing thousands of applications, the foundation concluded the experiment had failed operationally: AI-assisted submissions were often immature or irrelevant, and reviewing them consumed expert time. Policy v2.0 is framed as a pragmatic self-protection measure for NLnet's specific domain—digital infrastructure—rather than a general verdict on generative AI's quality, ethics or security. It takes effect immediately for calls with deadlines after 20 October 2026.
key_points: NLnet's policy v2.0 bans generative AI from writing proposals, except where it supports accessibility needs. For project development, LLMs and diffusion models are confined to read-only usage. The policy applies immediately to open calls with deadlines after 20 October 2026, including Restack and CodeSupply, whose first deadline is 3 November 2026.

NLnet says its earlier experiment with moderate, documented LLM use produced an avalanche of immature and low-relevance proposals. AI-involved proposals were generally lower quality and very taxing and demotivating for expert reviewers. Director Michiel Leenaars calls the new policy pragmatic self-protection, not a general judgment on AI quality, ethics or security.

Applicants who submitted early are urged to check compatibility with v2.0. Incompatible proposals can be revised and resubmitted through the normal application form, preferably citing the proposal ID, as many times as needed before the deadline. Applications written with AI before 20 October 2026 need not be resubmitted unless the proposed work itself violates the new policy.

Programmes in a concluding phase—notably NGI Zero Commons Fund, NGI Taler and Fediversity—get a transitional arrangement. Proposals still under evaluation will be treated under the previous v1.1 policy out of clemency, though applicants may voluntarily follow v2.0 with future applications in mind.
report.impact: For the AI industry, NLnet's move is a notable case of a grantmaker using operational evidence to tighten generative AI rules rather than making a broad ethical or technical claim. It signals that funders may increasingly treat AI-generated proposals and deliverables as a review burden, especially in specialised domains such as digital infrastructure. For developers, NLnet applicants must now keep AI use out of proposal writing, apart from accessibility support, and limit LLMs or diffusion models to read-only project use; early submissions may need revision. For regular users, the direct effect is limited, but the policy may influence norms around human-authored grant applications and AI disclosure in open-source funding.
report.tools: Follow NLnet's policy page and the Restack and CodeSupply call pages for deadlines and eligibility. Applicants can use plain-text or Markdown proposal templates, Git for version control, and documented accessibility tools where permitted. For context on transitional programmes, monitor NGI Zero Commons Fund, NGI Taler and Fediversity. No specific generative AI tool is recommended under the new policy.
